newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ATHLETICS-GEBRSELASSIE, MORCELI CHASE $1 MILLION PRIZE.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-GEBRSELASSIE, MORCELI CHASE $1 MILLION PRIZE.

text.p: Two of the world's finest distance runners warmed up on Thursday for a $1 million duel at the weekend which may provide a glimpse into the future of athletics.
Haile Gebrselassie of Ethiopia and Noureddine Morceli of Algeria compete over two miles in the Dutch town of Hengelo on Saturday, with the victor guaranteed the purse if he breaks eight minutes.
Head-to-head clashes are seen as a new opportunity to rekindle interest in athletics in today's crowded sporting market place.

"People like this kind of one-to-one competition, they want to know who is the strongest -- like it is with boxers." said Gebrselassie, world 5,000 metres record holder and Olympic 10,000 metres champion.
"It's a very, very good idea," agreed Morceli, world record holder for the mile, 1,500 and 2,000 metres.
"People are enthusiastic to see something new and it will be more exciting for the spectators and for all fans."
The double mile was chosen as a compromise between the two athletes' favoured distances and for the symbolic value of the eight-minute barrier.
"It could have the same impact as Roger Bannister breaking four minutes for the mile in 1954," said organiser Jos Hermans.
The current world record for the distance, held by Kenyan Daniel Komen, stands at eight minutes 3.54 seconds.
"We need good pacemakers, we need good weather. We need everything to be perfect if we are going to do it," said Gebrselassie, who once set the world mark at 8:07.46.
The two will run in a field of 11, with three "hares" charged with taking them to the necessary split times over 1,000 and 2,000 metres.
Organisers will instal a photo-finish and a full team of judges in case of a world record performance.
The Hengelo race is followed on Sunday by a similar duel in Toronto between Michael Johnson and Donovan Bailey over 150 metres, also with $1 million at stake.
Gebrselassie said it was a pity they had been arranged so close together. "People seem to have forgotten about us. Even in Ethiopia everyone was asking me about Mike Johnson and Donovan Bailey."

Morceli said that he would not let his friendship with Gebrselassie get in the way of a big-money opportunity. "Off the track we are friends -- but on the track even if you were competing against your own father you would not acknowledge him."
